content_voiceover: This diagram organizes coagulation as a series of enzyme-substrate complexes, which is a very useful way to think about it for boards. Starting on the upper left, the extrinsic tenase complex is factor VIIa plus tissue factor plus an anionic membrane plus calcium, and it acts on factor X as its substrate, converting it to Xa. Moving to the upper right, the intrinsic tenase complex is factor IXa plus factor VIIIa plus membrane plus calcium, and it also acts on factor X, generating more Xa, this is the amplification step that makes the intrinsic tenase far more efficient than the extrinsic tenase alone. In the center, the prothrombinase complex, factor Xa plus factor Va plus membrane plus calcium, acts on factor II, prothrombin, to generate thrombin, factor IIa. Finally, on the right, thrombin itself, together with thrombomodulin, membrane, and calcium, forms a complex that activates protein C, which is the body's natural anticoagulant brake on the system. At the bottom, thrombin's other major job is converting fibrinogen into cross-linked fibrin, completing clot formation. This complex-based framework helps you understand why cofactors like factor V and factor VIII are so clinically important, without them, these enzyme complexes lose most of their catalytic efficiency.
keypoints: Extrinsic tenase, VIIa plus tissue factor, activates factor X
Intrinsic tenase, IXa plus VIIIa, is the major amplifier of factor Xa generation
Prothrombinase, Xa plus Va, converts prothrombin to thrombin
Thrombin plus thrombomodulin activates protein C, the natural anticoagulant
keypoint_voiceover: Four key complexes to know. Extrinsic tenase and intrinsic tenase both generate Xa, prothrombinase generates thrombin, and the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex activates protein C to regulate the whole system.
